body:
Why energy systems require long-term finance

Power stations, renewable-energy installations, pipelines, substations and other energy infrastructure often require substantial expenditure before they can provide a service or earn revenue. Once commissioned, the facilities may operate for many years. This creates a need for long-term financing.

Finance may come from public investment, private equity, loans or other suitable funding arrangements. Public funds can support essential infrastructure or reduce specific risks, while private investors and lenders generally require confidence that the project can earn sufficient revenue to meet its obligations.

Capital cost and operating cost

Capital cost is expenditure on establishing or acquiring the facility, including major equipment and construction. Operating cost is expenditure incurred while running and maintaining it, such as fuel, routine maintenance and other continuing expenses.

These costs have different importance across technologies. A solar electricity project generally incurs substantial initial expenditure but requires no purchased sunlight as fuel. A fossil-fuel power station has capital costs as well as continuing fuel expenditure. Neither observation alone establishes which project will deliver electricity at the lowest overall cost.

The cost of capital is the cost of obtaining funds from lenders and investors. Higher borrowing rates or higher returns demanded by investors can make an otherwise similar project more expensive.

A low fuel cost does not automatically mean a low overall electricity cost. Capital expenditure, financing, maintenance, expected output and project risks also matter.

How risk affects financing

Investors and lenders assess whether a project can be completed and operated successfully and whether its purchasers will pay as agreed. Important basic risks include:

  • Construction risk: Delays or unexpected costs before the facility begins operating.
  • Resource risk: Actual generation or fuel availability differs from expectations.
  • Price risk: Electricity or fuel prices change in an unfavourable way.
  • Payment risk: The purchaser delays payment or fails to meet its obligations.
  • Regulatory and policy risk: Changes in applicable rules affect the project's expected revenue or cost.

A project with greater perceived risk may need to pay more for finance. Reliable contracts, clear rules, creditworthy purchasers and appropriate safeguards can reduce some risks, although they cannot eliminate every uncertainty.

What is a Power Purchase Agreement?

A Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) is a contract under which an electricity producer agrees to sell electricity to a purchaser on specified terms. Depending on the arrangement, the purchaser may be a distribution company or a large consumer.

A PPA commonly addresses the parties involved, the electricity or capacity being contracted, the agreed price or pricing mechanism, the contract period, delivery arrangements and the parties' obligations. The exact provisions vary among contracts.

For an electricity generator, a suitable long-term PPA can provide greater predictability about future sales and revenue. This may help the developer obtain finance. For the purchaser, it can secure a contractual source of electricity and reduce exposure to certain price fluctuations.

However, long-term contracts can also create obligations when market conditions change. A contract that gives price certainty today may offer less flexibility later, depending on its terms.

PPA price and retail electricity tariff

The price at which a generator sells electricity under a PPA is not necessarily the tariff paid by a household. Electricity delivered to a retail consumer can also involve transmission, distribution, service-related costs and applicable regulatory charges.

Likewise, a competitive renewable-energy bid price does not by itself represent the complete cost of delivering reliable electricity to every consumer at every hour.

Prelims focus

  • Capital cost is incurred in establishing an asset; operating cost arises during its operation.
  • Solar electricity does not require purchased sunlight as fuel, but it still has capital, financing and maintenance costs.
  • A PPA is a contract between an electricity producer and a purchaser.
  • Long-term PPAs can reduce revenue uncertainty but may also create continuing contractual obligations.
  • Trap: A generator's PPA price is not automatically equal to the retail tariff charged to households.

[International Renewable Energy Agency, Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024, published 2025, Executive Summary, discussion of capital intensity and cost of capital, p. 23; International Energy Agency, Advancing Decarbonisation through Clean Electricity Procurement, Executive Summary, section on Power Purchase Agreements; International Energy Agency, Scaling Up Private Finance for Clean Energy in Emerging and Developing Economies, Executive Summary, 2023; Solar Energy Corporation of India, Standard Power Purchase Agreement, contractual provisions, consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Energy Finance: Capital Costs, Investment Risk and Power Purchase Agreements

body:
Why carbon pricing is used

Activities that release greenhouse gases can impose environmental costs that are not fully reflected in the private cost of producing or consuming energy. Carbon pricing introduces a financial consequence associated with covered greenhouse-gas emissions. It gives firms and other regulated participants an incentive to reduce emissions when doing so is less costly than paying the applicable carbon price or meeting an equivalent obligation.

Carbon pricing does not directly guarantee that every product or energy service becomes cleaner. Its effect depends on the policy design, the activities covered and how firms and consumers respond.

Carbon tax and emissions trading

The 2 commonly discussed approaches are a carbon tax and an emissions trading system (ETS).

FeatureCarbon taxConventional cap-and-trade ETS
Main policy decisionSet a charge per unit of covered emissions.Set a limit on total covered emissions and create tradable allowances.
PriceSpecified by the tax arrangement.Generally determined through allowance trading, subject to market rules.
Emission quantityDepends on responses to the tax.Constrained by the defined allowance cap, subject to scheme provisions.
Basic incentiveReduce emissions to lower tax liability.Reduce emissions to lower allowance requirements or sell surplus allowances.

Both approaches attempt to make emissions more costly, but they operate differently. A carbon tax directly specifies a price. A conventional cap-and-trade system directly limits the covered quantity and allows trading to influence the price.

India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme

India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), 2023 was notified by the Ministry of Power on 28 June 2023 under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001, as amended in 2022. The scheme was amended in December 2023 to introduce an offset mechanism.

The scheme provides 2 distinct mechanisms:

Compliance mechanism

This mechanism applies to entities designated as obligated entities. It uses notified targets for greenhouse-gas emission intensity, meaning emissions per unit of specified output.

An obligated entity that performs better than its notified intensity target can become eligible to receive carbon credit certificates under the scheme's rules. An entity that fails to meet the target must surrender banked or purchased carbon credit certificates corresponding to its excess emission intensity multiplied by its output.

Offset mechanism

The offset mechanism permits eligible non-obligated entities to register voluntary projects that reduce, avoid or remove greenhouse-gas emissions relative to an established baseline. Subject to the applicable methodology, validation and verification requirements, these activities can qualify for carbon credit certificates.

Why emission intensity matters

Emission intensity measures greenhouse-gas emissions relative to production. It is different from the total quantity of emissions.

Intensity and total emissions

Suppose a factory initially emits 100 tonnes of greenhouse gases while producing 100 units of output. Its emission intensity is 1 tonne per unit. Later, it emits 120 tonnes while producing 150 units. Its intensity falls to 0.8 tonne per unit, even though its total emissions rise from 100 tonnes to 120 tonnes.

This illustrates why an intensity-based baseline-and-credit scheme must not be described automatically as a fixed absolute cap on total national emissions.

Important institutions

The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) is the administrator of the CCTS. The Grid Controller of India serves as the registry operator for the Indian Carbon Market, and the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) regulates trading activities under the framework.

These are different institutional roles. Administration of the scheme, management of certificate records and regulation of trading are not identical functions.

Connection with energy prices and fairness

Carbon pricing may increase the cost of emissions-intensive production. Businesses may respond by improving efficiency, changing fuels, adopting cleaner technologies or adjusting their prices. The burden passed to consumers depends on market conditions and the policy's coverage.

For this reason, carbon-pricing policy can interact with affordability and just-transition measures. Governments may consider targeted assistance for vulnerable consumers or affected workers, while preserving incentives for cleaner production.

Status and data period: The dates above refer to the original 2023 notification and its December 2023 amendment. The institutional roles and mechanism descriptions follow BEE's published framework consulted on 16 November 2026. No claim is made here about a particular current carbon-credit trading price or transaction volume.

Prelims focus

  • India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme was notified on 28 June 2023.
  • The December 2023 amendment introduced the offset mechanism.
  • The 2 mechanisms are compliance and offset.
  • The compliance mechanism uses notified greenhouse-gas emission-intensity targets for obligated entities.
  • BEE administers the scheme; Grid Controller of India operates the registry; CERC regulates trading.
  • Trap: Lower emissions per unit of output do not necessarily mean lower total emissions.

[Ministry of Power, Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, 2023, Gazette Notification S.O. 2825(E), dated 28 June 2023; Bureau of Energy Efficiency, Detailed Procedure for Offset Mechanism, About the Offset Mechanism, paragraphs I–IV; Bureau of Energy Efficiency, Carbon Market, sections 4.3 and 4.4 and institutional responsibilities, consulted 16 November 2026; World Bank, Carbon Pricing Assessment and Decision Making: A Guide to Adopting a Carbon Price, sections 1.2.1 and 1.2.2.]

pictures.alt: CCTS compliance assesses obligated entities against intensity targets; offsets assess voluntary projects against a baseline, with conditional certificates.
pictures.caption: The CCTS compliance and offset mechanisms have different participants and functions.

title: Carbon Pricing and India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme

body:
Why consumer protection is part of energy policy

Energy policy affects people not only through the quantity of electricity or fuel available but also through the reliability, price and quality of the service they receive. An energy system cannot be judged solely by the capacity of its power stations or the cost of new projects.

A consumer may face an incorrect bill, delayed connection, defective meter or prolonged interruption. Consumer-protection rules establish responsibilities for electricity suppliers and provide procedures for resolving grievances.

Consumer protection under the Electricity Act, 2003

The Electricity Act, 2003 contains several provisions relevant to the supply of electricity and consumer rights.

  • Section 43: Provides for a distribution licensee's duty to supply electricity on an owner's or occupier's application. The Act sets a general limit of 1 month from receipt of the application, with Commission-set periods for network extension, new substations or unserved areas and exceptions under Section 44 for events beyond the licensee's control.
  • Section 57: Enables the regulatory commission to specify standards of performance and provides for compensation when a licensee fails to meet applicable standards, with compensation determined after giving the licensee a reasonable opportunity to be heard and payable within 90 days of determination.
  • Section 42(5): Requires distribution licensees to establish a forum for redressal of consumer grievances in accordance with the State Commission's guidelines.
  • Section 42(6): Allows a consumer whose grievance has not been redressed through the forum to approach the Ombudsman appointed or designated by the State Commission.

Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules, 2020

The Ministry of Power notified the Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules, 2020 on 31 December 2020. These rules address matters such as electricity connections, metering, billing, reliability, standards of performance, compensation and grievance redressal.

Under the applicable rules and regulations, electricity suppliers are expected to follow prescribed service standards. Compensation may be payable when specified standards are violated. The exact entitlement depends on the nature of the failure and the relevant provisions; compensation is not automatically identical for every interruption or complaint.

How a grievance is addressed

A consumer ordinarily begins by raising the problem through the distribution licensee's designated complaint-handling arrangements. If the complaint remains unresolved, the consumer can use the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum (CGRF) process established under the applicable regulations. A consumer aggrieved by non-redressal through the forum may then make a representation to the Electricity Ombudsman as provided by Section 42(6) and the applicable rules.

The forum and the Ombudsman are part of consumer grievance redressal. They should not be confused with the Electricity Regulatory Commission's broader functions, such as determining regulated tariffs.

Gujarat's consumer and tariff framework

In Gujarat, the Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission (GERC) regulates electricity tariffs and issues relevant consumer-protection regulations within its statutory jurisdiction. Distribution licensees, including DGVCL in its authorised area, provide electricity service under the applicable tariff orders and regulatory requirements.

A consumer's electricity charges must therefore be understood with reference to the applicable consumer category, tariff order, billing conditions and authorised government levies. A price quoted for one category or one financial year should not be assumed to apply universally.

Bringing the 3 policy areas together

Energy security asks whether adequate energy can be obtained reliably and at a manageable cost. It is strengthened through diversification, appropriate reserves, efficient demand and resilient infrastructure.

Just energy transition asks whether changes in production and consumption treat workers, communities and consumers fairly. It requires attention to employment, skills, livelihoods, consultation and the unequal distribution of costs.

Energy finance and pricing ask how infrastructure is funded, how investors and utilities recover justified costs, and how prices influence producers and consumers. Tariffs, subsidies, PPAs and carbon-pricing instruments perform different functions within this broader system.

A successful policy must consider these questions together. Keeping electricity prices artificially low without funding the difference can weaken the finances of a distribution utility. Raising prices without protecting vulnerable households can reduce affordability. Expanding cleaner generation without planning for affected workers can produce regional hardship.

No single measure solves every energy-policy problem. Strategic oil stocks cannot replace worker retraining; a carbon price cannot replace consumer grievance redressal; and a subsidy cannot by itself guarantee reliable infrastructure. The appropriate response depends on the problem being addressed.

Prelims focus

  • Section 43 of the Electricity Act, 2003 concerns the duty to supply electricity on request, subject to statutory conditions.
  • Section 57 concerns standards of performance and compensation.
  • Section 42(5) provides for consumer grievance forums; Section 42(6) provides for representation to the Ombudsman.
  • The Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules, 2020 were notified on 31 December 2020.
  • GERC is the electricity regulatory commission for Gujarat.
  • Trap: The consumer grievance forum and Ombudsman are not the same as the body responsible for determining electricity tariffs.

[Electricity Act, 2003, Sections 42(5), 42(6), 43 and 57, India Code, consulted 16 November 2026; Ministry of Power, Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules, 2020, notified 31 December 2020; Press Information Bureau, Rules to Protect Consumer Rights in the Power Sector, 15 March 2022; Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission, Tariff Orders and regulatory functions, consulted 16 November 2026; International Energy Agency, Glossary, entry on Energy Security; International Labour Organization, Guidelines for a Just Transition towards Environmentally Sustainable Economies and Societies for All, 2015.]

pictures.caption: Electricity consumers have a structured route for addressing unresolved grievances.

pictures.alt: Energy security, just transition and finance converge on reliable, affordable, environmentally responsible and socially fair energy services.
pictures.caption: Energy policy must jointly consider secure supply, fair treatment and sustainable financing.

title: Consumer Protection and Balancing Energy Security, Fairness and Cost
